The 80 / 20 rule, measured honestly

A few causes do most of the work.

Across economics, language, sound and software, ~80% of effects tend to flow from ~20% of causes. This is an interactive field guide: test the claim on your own typing, words, camera and voice — and watch inequality emerge from nothing.

A classic Pareto curve — bars sorted, cumulative line, 80% mark
80 / 20

A label, not a law

The real split might be 90/10 or 70/30 — and the numbers needn't sum to 100.

1896

Pareto's discovery

~80% of Italy's land sat with ~20% of its people. The shape kept recurring.

round(n×0.2)

Fixed in advance

We pin the top 20% first, then measure their share — never cherry-pick.

Jump into an experiment

Eight live tests of the same lopsided shape. Each shows the activity first, then the full math beneath it.

Where 80/20 shows up in the real world

The same shape across economics, language, health and more. Bars sorted largest→smallest, the white line is the running cumulative total, the dashed line marks 80%.

Figures are approximate and illustrative — drawn from commonly cited reports and classic studies to show the characteristic shape, not exact values.

The principle, in depth
Experiment 01 · Letters

Your keyboard, heat-mapped

Do the top 20% of letters — five of the twenty-six — really account for 80% of your keystrokes? Type something, or keep the typical-English view, and measure it.

—

—

26

Darker keys are pressed more often; the outlined keys are the “vital few.”

Cumulative keystrokes — the Pareto curve

Letters sorted most→least used. The line climbs steeply, then flattens.

Type something to test the 80/20 rule on your own text.

How it works & the math
Experiment 02 · Zipf's law

Words: the cleanest 80/20 of all

Rank whole words instead of letters and the concentration sharpens dramatically. A handful of function words — the, of, and, to — carry most of any text. This is the classic case: Zipf's law.

—
top 20% of unique words
—
of all words written

Type or paste some text to test it.

The Zipf signature — a straight line on log–log axes

Each dot is one word: its rank (most→least common) versus how often it appears, both on logarithmic scales. The dashed line is the ideal frequency ∝ 1/rank.

Zipf's law, in depth
Experiment 03 · Randomness

Monkeys: order from pure chance

No language at all — we hammer random keys (letters + the spacebar) and split the gibberish into “words.” Even so, a few short accidental words dominate. Concentration emerging from nothing (Miller's monkeys).

        The measure · Concentration
        
Lorenz curve & the Gini coefficient

        

          The Lorenz curve plots cumulative share of the “stuff” against cumulative share of the
          population. The more it bows below the line of equality, the more concentrated things
          are — and the Gini coefficient sums that up in a single number. Drag to vary it.
